headline: Sea Bright Rocks, First Light: Blues Chew Bunker While the Bass Play Hooky
subhead: The jetty rats are getting their arms worked over by cocktail blues while the stripers sit this one out until dark.
body_markdown:
Quarter to six this morning I'm out on the north jetty at Sea Bright, coffee going cold in the rod holder, and there's already three guys ahead of me picking their way out over the wet rocks with headlamps still on. Nobody's talking. That's how you know something's happening — jetty rats go quiet when the birds are already working before the sun's even up.

And they were working. A bunker school the size of a football field was getting worked from underneath, and every few minutes the whole thing would erupt — blues busting through, gulls dropping on the scraps, that unmistakable sound of water getting slapped by something angry. Guys were throwing bunker spoons and topwater poppers into the edges of it, not even into the thick of it, because you don't need to. The blues were following the bait right up against the rocks. Cocktails mostly, a few pushing three and four pounds, and enough of them that by seven o'clock everybody out there had bent a rod more than once.

We flagged this one a few days back — said the bunker schools would keep spreading with this stable high-pressure stretch and that cocktail blues in the back bays and along the beachfront would spike because of it. Well, here it is. Sea Bright's had it two mornings running now, and word from Belmar is the same thing's setting up off the Ninth Avenue jetty and down toward Spring Lake. If you see gulls sitting low and nervous over a patch of water at dawn, don't wait around — paddle out or walk fast, because these schools don't sit still long once the sun climbs.

Here's the honest part, though. The bass have mostly checked out on us. Ocean temps are sitting in the mid-70s out past the bar — 75.9 at the buoy off the Bight — and that's summer-pattern water, which means stripers are doing what they do this time of year: going nocturnal and hugging deeper, cooler structure. I picked at a few schoolies working the Manasquan Inlet rocks two nights ago on the last of the outgoing, throwing a black Gibbs pencil popper along the north jetty face in that skinny water where the current pinches through, but it was one here, one there, nothing you'd call a pattern. If you want a crack at a bass right now, fish it dark — an hour before first light through sunrise, working the jetty rocks at Manasquan or the Shark River Inlet on the last two hours of the ebb, when bait gets flushed out through the gut and stripers stack up to ambush it. Swimming plugs and darters worked slow along the rocks, not bucktails — the water's too warm for them to chase hard, so you want something they can eat without working for it.

Fluke are still the more dependable daytime play. The Shark River channel and the deeper holes inside Manasquan Inlet have been giving up keeper fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming and the top of the outgoing when the current's got some push but hasn't gone slack. Depths of 15 to 25 feet inside the inlet channels have been the sweet spot — deep enough to hold cooler water, structured enough to hold bait. Nothing spectacular, but a couple keepers for a morning's work is a fair trade this time of year.

Porgies are thick on the nearshore structure off Belmar and Manasquan — the usual reefs and rockpiles in 30 to 50 feet — and they'll keep any kid or first-timer busy while the adults chase the blues. Bloodworms or clam on a high-low rig, nothing fancy needed. And the back bays behind Shark River and the Manasquan River are stuffed with snapper blues right now, which is good news if you've got a young angler who wants nonstop action on tiny gold spoons or spearing under a bobber off the docks.

What I'm watching for the next week is whether that bunker push holds. This high-pressure stretch we've had — light winds, settled seas, the surf running maybe three to four feet at a longer period — is exactly the kind of pattern that keeps bunker schools moving steady along this stretch instead of scattering. If it holds, I'd expect the blitz action to keep sliding both directions from Sea Bright, hitting Asbury Park and down through Belmar and Spring Lake over the coming days. Worth checking the jetties at first light regardless of where you live on this stretch — the birds will tell you before anything else does.

As for albies — too early to promise anything, but with this much bait sitting inshore and water temps where they are, I wouldn't be shocked if the first false albacore showed up scouting the Manasquan Inlet rips by the end of the month, a couple weeks ahead of the usual calendar. I'll be watching the birds and the boils same as always. For now, if you want a bent rod at dawn, the blues are your best bet — and they're not shy about it.
